posts.title: How Borrowed for the Holidays Became My Christmas Story
posts.excerpt: I wanted to write a Christmas novella that felt warm, romantic, a little cheesy, and completely ready for the holidays. Then August and Rafe showed up.
posts.content:
I wanted to write a Christmas story.

That was really where Borrowed for the Holidays began.

I knew I wanted something I could release right before Christmas. I wanted a novella rather than a full-length novel, something readers could curl up with during the holiday season and disappear into for a little while.

And from the beginning, I knew exactly what kind of Christmas story I wanted it to be.

Warm.

Romantic.

Festive.

A little cheesy.

Maybe even a little cliché.

Basically, I wanted my version of a Hallmark Christmas movie.

And I'm completely okay with that.

First came Christmas

There is something about Christmas that seems made for romance stories.

The lights. The decorations. Small downtown streets dressed for the season. Families coming together. Traditions resurfacing. People returning home. Feelings becoming harder to ignore when everyone around you seems determined to make everything merry and bright.

It's practically begging for two people to fall in love.

So when I started thinking about writing a novella specifically for the Christmas season, I didn't want to fight any of those familiar elements.

I wanted to embrace them.

I wasn't interested in writing a Christmas story that tried desperately to prove it was different from every Christmas romance that came before it.

I wanted the coziness.

I wanted the romance.

I wanted those moments where readers can probably see what's coming and still want it to happen anyway.

Sometimes that's part of the fun.

Then came Georgetown

Once I knew I wanted to write a Christmas novella, I needed somewhere to put it.

That part came pretty naturally.

Most of my novels tend to live somewhere in or around the Austin, Texas area. There's something about Central Texas that keeps pulling my imagination back there, and maybe part of that is because Austin is somewhere I hope to call home myself one day.

For Borrowed for the Holidays, though, I wanted to move just outside Austin.

Georgetown felt right.

It gave me the setting I wanted for this particular story. It could still exist within the broader Central Texas world I enjoy writing about while giving this novella its own personality.

And once I imagined Georgetown at Christmastime, the story started becoming much easier to see.

I could picture the lights.

I could picture the decorated streets.

I could picture my characters walking through it all while trying very hard not to acknowledge whatever was obviously developing between them.

That's when a Christmas novella started becoming Borrowed for the Holidays.

And then August and Rafe showed up

Every story eventually reaches the moment when an idea stops being an idea and starts belonging to actual people.

For this story, those people became August and Rafe.

Once they appeared, the story wasn't simply about writing something festive anymore.

It became their Christmas.

The more I thought about them, the more I wanted to know how they would fit together. What would draw them toward each other? What would make things complicated? What would they be afraid to admit? And, because I'm writing a romance, exactly how much could I make them go through before finally giving readers the moment they've been waiting for?

That's the fun part.

Characters have a way of taking a fairly simple premise and making it feel bigger because suddenly there are emotions attached to everything.

August and Rafe did that for me.

Yes, it feels like Hallmark

I'm not going to pretend this story isn't leaning into some familiar Christmas romance territory.

It absolutely is.

There are parts of Borrowed for the Holidays that feel like they belong in a Hallmark Christmas movie.

There are moments that might be cheesy.

There are probably things readers will call cliché.

And you know what?

I'm excited about all of it.

Sometimes we treat "predictable" like it's automatically a criticism of romance. But there are certain stories we return to precisely because we know how they're supposed to make us feel.

We know the Christmas lights are coming.

We know somebody is probably going to catch feelings they weren't planning to catch.

We know there will be misunderstandings, longing, romantic tension, and at least a few moments where we want to yell at the characters to just admit what they want.

And yes, we know we're heading toward a happy ending.

That's not a problem for me.

That's the promise.

Making that kind of Christmas story mine

Of course, I don't want to simply recreate a Christmas movie I've already watched.

The fun is taking that familiar holiday-romance feeling and filtering it through the kinds of characters and relationships I enjoy writing.

I get to create a Christmas romance where two men get to be at the center of all that holiday magic.

They get the lights.

They get the longing.

They get the ridiculous romantic complications.

They get the moments that make you smile because you know exactly where this is going.

And they get the kind of big, warm, satisfying romance that holiday stories have been giving audiences for years.

That's something I'm genuinely excited to write.

A little escape for the holidays

Not every story has to carry the weight of the world.

Sometimes I want to write something that makes you think deeply about identity, faith, relationships, or the complicated parts of being human.

And sometimes I want to give you a Christmas romance.

Borrowed for the Holidays gets to be that.

There can still be real emotions underneath it. August and Rafe are still going to have things to figure out about themselves and each other.

But I also want this book to feel like an escape.

I want it to feel like putting on your favorite Christmas movie even though you've already watched it five times.

I want you to settle in knowing there's romance ahead.

I want you rooting for August and Rafe.

I want you smiling at the cheesy parts instead of apologizing for enjoying them.

Most of all, I want Borrowed for the Holidays to feel like Christmas.

I can't wait for you to meet them

It's funny to think that this started with something as simple as wanting to release a novella right before Christmas.

Then I found Georgetown.

Then August arrived.

Then Rafe.

And suddenly I had a story I couldn't wait to tell.

So yes, Borrowed for the Holidays might be a little cheesy.

It might embrace a cliché or two.

It might make you feel like you've wandered into a gay Hallmark Christmas movie set in Georgetown, Texas.

That's kind of the point.

I'm having a lot of fun creating this one, and I cannot wait until August and Rafe's story is no longer just living in my head and on my screen.

I can't wait to share their Christmas with you.

posts.title: How Interim Was Born in a Quiet Moment at Work
posts.excerpt: Sometimes a story arrives when you least expect it. Interim started with two names during a quiet moment at work and quickly became something I couldn’t stop writing.
posts.content:
Sometimes a story doesn't wait until you're ready to write it.

It doesn't care whether you're sitting at your desk with your laptop open, your playlist going, and everything perfectly arranged for a productive writing session.

Sometimes it just shows up.

That's exactly how Interim began.

It started with two names

I was at work during one of those slow stretches where there wasn't much happening. I was standing around waiting, my mind wandering the way it tends to do when there's finally a little room for it to wander.

Then two names came into my head.

Asher.

Brynne.

That was it.

No elaborate plot. No character profiles. No outline. I didn't know what their story was supposed to be or why these two names had suddenly taken up residence in my brain.

But they wouldn't leave.

I started wondering who Asher was. Then I wondered who Brynne was. Why did they know each other? What did they want? What was happening in their lives?

Those questions turned into a few lines.

A few lines became more.

Before I knew it, this random idea that showed up while I was passing time at work had turned into three chapters.

Apparently, I was writing another book.

Meeting Asher Callahan

The more I wrote, the more Asher Callahan began revealing himself to me.

He's an interim marketing director at a thriving nonprofit. He's ambitious, driven by purpose, and good at what he does.

But underneath all of that competence is someone carrying more than he probably should.

Asher is dealing with burnout, professional pressure, expectations, relationships, and the uncomfortable realization that being capable of handling everything doesn't necessarily mean you should.

That tension immediately interested me.

What happens when someone who is used to being in control reaches a point where control isn't enough anymore?

And what happens when love enters the picture at exactly the wrong, or maybe exactly the right, time?

Then Zeph walked in

Asher's world shifts when he meets Zephyrion "Zeph" Ward, a magnetic new staff member who wasn't part of Asher's plans.

And I love characters who weren't part of the plan.

Zeph complicates things. His presence begins changing Asher's understanding of what he wants, what he's willing to risk, and how much of himself he's actually willing to let another person see.

But romance isn't the only relationship being challenged.

There's also Brynne Douglas, Asher's best friend and co-worker.

Remember that second name that appeared in my head?

She became much more important to the story than simply being Asher's friend.

As Asher begins changing, the relationships around him have to change too. And sometimes the people who have known one version of us the longest aren't prepared for the version of us we're becoming.

Ambition versus authenticity

As Interim started taking shape, I realized I was writing about something bigger than workplace pressure or an unexpected romance.

I was writing about ambition.

More specifically, I was writing about what happens when ambition begins competing with authenticity.

There's nothing inherently wrong with wanting more. I understand wanting to build something, accomplish something, become better at what you do, and create a life that feels meaningful.

But what happens when you're so focused on where you're going that you stop asking whether the person getting there is still you?

That's one of the questions sitting underneath Asher's journey.

Friendships change too

Another theme that emerged unexpectedly was friendship.

We talk a lot about romantic relationships changing, ending, or growing apart. We don't always talk about how painful it can be when friendships shift.

Sometimes nobody is necessarily the villain.

People grow.

Priorities change.

New relationships enter our lives.

Things that once worked between two people suddenly don't work the same way anymore.

Asher and Brynne's friendship gives me a chance to explore some of that complexity alongside the romance developing elsewhere in his life.

A story I wasn't looking for

That's probably my favorite thing about how Interim came into existence.

I wasn't looking for it.

I wasn't trying to come up with my next brilliant book idea. I wasn't brainstorming characters or searching for inspiration.

I was standing at work.

Then Asher showed up.

Then Brynne.

Then Zeph.

And suddenly there was a story asking me to pay attention.

Maybe that's one of the strangest parts of being a writer. Inspiration doesn't always arrive dramatically. Sometimes there's no lightning bolt and no perfect creative environment.

Sometimes your imagination quietly hands you two names and waits to see what you're going to do with them.

I followed those names.

Now they're leading me into a story about burnout, ambition, friendship, authenticity, control, and unexpected love.

Not bad for a quiet moment at work.

posts.title: Writing Through Church Hurt: Uncloseted Hearts Is Coming
posts.excerpt: Writing Uncloseted Hearts has forced me to revisit church hurt, faith, identity, and what healing looks like when the wounds came from somewhere that was supposed to feel safe.
posts.content:
Writing Uncloseted Hearts has been hard.

Part of that comes with writing the second book in a series. Closeted Hearts introduced the world of Hearts Unveiled, and I want the next story to feel like it belongs in that world while still standing firmly on its own.

But there is another reason this book has been difficult to write.

This one gets personal.

Writing about church hurt

Uncloseted Hearts follows Evan, a character introduced in Closeted Hearts, as he deals with the aftermath of being hurt by a community that was supposed to love him.

His story isn't my story. Evan is his own character, with his own experiences, choices, relationships, and journey.

But I know church hurt.

I know what it feels like when a place that talks constantly about love doesn't feel loving anymore. I know the confusion of trying to separate God from the people who claim to speak for God. I know what it is like to wonder whether there is still a place for you in a faith community when being fully yourself seems to come with conditions.

And I know what it feels like to carry those wounds long after you've left the place where you received them.

When faith and identity collide

For a long time, being gay and being Christian felt like two identities I was expected to keep fighting against each other.

There were prayers for change. There was shame. There were questions I was afraid to ask out loud. There were moments in worship when I wondered whether God saw me, heard me, or even wanted me there.

Those experiences don't disappear simply because you eventually begin accepting yourself.

Sometimes your mind moves forward before your heart does.

Sometimes you leave the harmful theology but still hear its voice.

Sometimes you know intellectually that you don't believe something anymore, but part of you is still afraid it might be true.

That tension became important to Evan's story.

Healing isn't a straight line

I didn't want Uncloseted Hearts to tell a neat story where someone gets hurt, learns an important lesson, and suddenly everything is fine.

That's not how healing has worked for me.

Healing has come in layers.

There are things I thought I had completely moved beyond that resurfaced while writing this book. There have been memories I didn't expect to revisit and emotions I didn't expect fictional scenes to bring back.

I've had moments when writing Evan made me angry.

I've had moments when it made me emotional.

But I've also had moments when writing him brought unexpected peace.

That's when I realized I wasn't only writing from the wounds anymore. I was beginning to write from some of the scars.

What happens after the hurt?

One of the questions underneath Uncloseted Hearts is what happens when the institution that helped shape your understanding of God also becomes responsible for some of your deepest spiritual wounds.

Do you walk away from faith completely?

Do you rebuild it?

Do you redefine what faith means?

Can you trust another church community?

Can you trust yourself?

And perhaps most importantly, can you stop seeing yourself through the eyes of people who taught you that something fundamental about you needed to change?

Evan has to wrestle with those questions.

I have wrestled with some of them too.

More than a story about pain

I don't want Uncloseted Hearts to simply be a story about church hurt.

It's also about what comes afterward.

It's about reclaiming identity. It's about questioning beliefs you inherited and deciding what you actually believe. It's about learning that leaving a particular version of faith doesn't necessarily mean abandoning God.

And because this is still a romance, it's also about letting someone love you when experience has taught you to keep parts of yourself protected.

There is pain in Evan's story, but there is also love.

There is anger, but there is hope.

There are questions without immediate answers.

There is healing that doesn't happen all at once.

For anyone who has been hurt by church

If you've ever been hurt by a church, especially because of who you are, I hope something in Evan's journey feels familiar.

I hope you see that questioning what you were taught doesn't automatically make you faithless.

I hope you know that rebuilding your relationship with faith, whatever that ultimately looks like for you, doesn't have to happen according to someone else's timeline.

And I hope you know that the people who rejected you don't get the final word on your worth.

Uncloseted Hearts is becoming one of the most personal things I've written, even though Evan's story isn't mine.

Maybe that's what fiction can do.

It gives us enough distance to create something new while still allowing us to tell the truth about feelings we've carried for years.

That's what I'm trying to do with Evan.

I'm writing about church hurt, but I'm also writing about what happens when hurt doesn't get to be the end of the story.

posts.title: Why I Wrote Closeted Hearts
posts.excerpt: Closeted Hearts began during a difficult season of my life, when I needed somewhere to put everything I was carrying.
posts.content:
Some books begin because you have a story you are determined to tell. Closeted Hearts began because I needed somewhere to go.

I started writing it during a really difficult season in my life. Mentally and emotionally, I was carrying a lot, and writing gave me something else to focus on. I wasn't sitting down with some grand plan to write a novel or launch a series. At first, I simply needed an escape.

Then a question came to me: What if there was a gay romance between two men who worked at a church?

That question became Closeted Hearts.

A world I understood

The idea interested me because I understood the world surrounding these characters. I had worked in a church before. I knew the culture, the language, the expectations, and the complicated relationship that can exist between faith, identity, and belonging.

I also understood what it felt like to wrestle with parts of yourself that you weren't sure could exist together.

Closeted Hearts is fiction. The events of the book did not happen to me. But many of the emotions underneath the story are very real.

The fear of being seen.

The desire to be known and loved completely.

The tension of loving God while learning that loving yourself shouldn't require rejecting your queerness.

Those feelings gave me something real to build the fictional story around.

Writing queer characters who get to be more

For years, I felt as though faith and being gay were two parts of myself that weren't supposed to occupy the same room. Eventually, I reached a point where I stopped believing I had to choose.

That realization has influenced the kinds of stories I want to tell.

I want LGBTQ+ characters to get more than stories about suffering. I want them to fall in love. I want them to make mistakes. I want them to laugh, argue, heal, question themselves, find community, and figure out what they actually want from life.

And when faith belongs in a particular story, I want there to be room for that complexity too.

Not every book I write will center faith. Not every character will share my experiences or beliefs. But I do want my stories to make room for people who haven't always seen themselves treated as fully human in the stories they've been given.

Who I wrote Closeted Hearts for

I wrote Closeted Hearts for readers who understand what it means to hide something important about themselves.

I wrote it for the person who has sat in a church pew wondering whether everyone around them would still embrace them if they knew the whole truth.

I wrote it for people who have wondered whether love, faith, identity, and authenticity can exist together.

And I wrote it for people who simply want to read a romance about two men trying to figure themselves out while also figuring out each other.

The story became something bigger

What started as an escape eventually became something I cared deeply about.

Writing Closeted Hearts helped me understand why storytelling matters so much to me. Sometimes fiction gives us a safe place to explore questions we haven't figured out how to ask anywhere else. Sometimes characters say things we are still learning how to say ourselves.

And sometimes the story you begin because you need an escape becomes the story that helps you understand yourself a little better.

That's what Closeted Hearts became for me.

It started with one question about two men working at a church.

It became a story about being seen, being known, finding love, and discovering what can happen when you finally stop believing that the truest parts of yourself need to remain hidden.
